video_title: Is AI 'Safety' Talk Really a Regulatory Moat Against Cheap Chinese Models? - Uneasy Money
gist: Three crypto builders (host Kane, security co-host Taylor Mahan, and Deli Ventures founding partner Tommy) dissect the collapse of the Clarity market-structure bill in the Senate and conclude the industry will now be governed by SEC/CFTC rulemaking rather than law. The bulk of the episode argues that OpenAI's and Anthropic's calls to 'slow down' are a mix of pre-IPO financial hygiene, unit-economics relief and an explicit regulatory moat against cheap Chinese open-source models, and that the real edge is owning your own AI stack. They close with an $8M Gnosis Safe exploit, SDNY insider-trading charges against Robinhood engineers, and Wyoming's stable-token commission dropping Layer Zero for Chainlink.

insights.claim: The Clarity crypto market-structure bill died in the Senate without even reaching 50 votes, after an industry lobbying effort widely described as costing around $100 million.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Legislative certainty is off the table for this cycle; anyone underwriting US crypto risk on the assumption of a statute has to reprice to agency-driven rules.
insights.quote: we spent a hundred million dollars on this

insights.claim: With the Clarity bill dead, the SEC and CFTC are expected to use their own comment-letter and rulemaking authority to push as much crypto enablement as they legally can.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Watch SEC/CFTC rule proposals, not Congress, as the next catalyst for tokenized-securities and exchange-listing products.
insights.quote: it looks like based on the SEC and the CFTC comments that they're about to unleash as much uh enablement as they possibly can

insights.claim: Relying on regulators rather than legislation leaves crypto in a fragile equilibrium: the same discretionary rulemaking power that is friendly today was hostile three years ago and can flip with the next administration.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Price a policy-reversal premium into US-domiciled crypto businesses; agency-granted permissions are revocable in a way statutes are not.
insights.quote: setting setting the agenda for an entire industry is a very fragile equilibrium right like it was fragile when they were trying to kill us now they're not trying to that's also fragile

insights.claim: Clarity failed largely because it lost negotiating momentum — unlike the GENIUS stablecoin bill, which had constant iteration, back-and-forth and public debate right up to passage.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Use visible legislative iteration (markups, public concessions) as the leading indicator for whether a crypto bill will pass; silence is a kill signal.
insights.quote: I kind of forgot about clarity when it came back

insights.claim: The ethics provisions, not the technical market-structure provisions, were what stalled Clarity, and the concessions negotiated away did not actually resolve the ethics objections.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Any revived bill must address presidential-conflict-of-interest provisions head-on; repeating the same concession structure likely fails again.
insights.quote: I'm not actually sure if the concessions that were made were actually actually addressed the ethics concerns

insights.claim: Two rounds of major concessions followed by failure suggests bad-faith negotiation by opponents rather than genuine policy disagreement.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: If the opposition was never winnable, the industry's next play is electoral rather than legislative — which is exactly what the panel advocates.
insights.quote: it seems like there was like a massive concession at one point and then again this Sunday and it still didn't pass. Which makes me feel like there's got to be some bad faith elements to this.

insights.claim: The Trump family's own crypto ventures — the Trump and Melania memecoins and World Liberty Financial — are named as the decisive reason Clarity became unpassable.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: Insider-enrichment optics are now a direct legislative cost to the whole sector; expect future bills to stall while those ventures remain active.
insights.quote: honestly I think Trump and Melania and the shitcoins and world liberty I think all of that

insights.claim: Crypto markets did not sell off on the bill's failure because participants believe three things: the SEC and CFTC will enable crypto anyway, angry informed voters will punish opposing senators, and the sector grows 10x regardless of legislation.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Legislative headlines have lost their ability to move crypto prices; positioning off DC news flow has weaker expected value than it did a year ago.
insights.quote: crypto is going to grow another 10x and it's not really going to matter like it'll be enabled later on

insights.claim: Stablecoin adoption is the Trojan horse for the rest of crypto, so leaving yield-bearing stablecoin rules unresolved is a concrete net negative that slows the sector's main adoption vector.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Yield-bearing stablecoin issuers face continued legal ambiguity; distribution partners (banks, brokerages) will stay slow to integrate.
insights.quote: there is no question that stable coin adoption is uh like a a bit of a Trojan horse for the rest of crypto

insights.claim: The unanswered question Clarity would have settled is how close a token can get to pseudo-equity — whether a tokenized enterprise can pay dividends and what rights it can carry.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Tokenized-equity and revenue-share token designs stay in legal limbo, keeping that category smaller than the RWA narrative implies until an SEC rule lands.
insights.quote: are you allowed to pay dividends are you allowed to like how how close to like pseudo equity can you get

insights.claim: Clarity's failure is a talent headwind: a founder six months from launching who was weighing AI against crypto loses the newly opened opportunity set that might have pulled them to crypto.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Expect continued founder migration toward AI; deal flow quality for crypto venture funds is the thing to monitor, not token prices.

insights.claim: Crypto's structural embedding in pension funds, RIAs and IRAs is why the panel is not heartbroken about the bill failing now, whereas the same failure a year or two ago would have been critical.
insights.speaker: Kane (host) and Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Allocation channels, not legislation, are now the durable bid; distribution wins already banked are hard for any future administration to unwind.
insights.quote: It's in pension funds. It's in RAS. It's in IAS. Like it's everywhere.

insights.claim: Starting a DeFi project today means competing against NASDAQ-listed entities pursuing the same business, a materially more competitive environment than 2018-2020.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: New DeFi entrants face lower legal risk but much lower variance of outcome; the asymmetric returns that existed pre-2021 have been competed away.
insights.quote: today, you turn up and you're competing against like listed entities on the NASDAQ that are trying to do the same thing as you

insights.claim: The anti-crypto-army political position is negative expected value: it wins zero votes from normies while creating roughly 30 million motivated single-issue opponents, a lesson Democrats learned in the last election.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Explicit anti-crypto campaigning is unlikely to return at scale, capping the tail risk of a hostile legislative swing even without a bill.
insights.quote: it's the most negative EV possible thing that you could do because a normie just does not care

insights.claim: The expected populist backlash against crypto never materialized because the actual popular sentiment was that people wanted to trade, not that they resented traders.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Retail speculation demand is a political constituency, not a political liability — relevant to how aggressively exchanges and brokers can expand product.
insights.quote: the populist uprising was like people wanted to trade

insights.claim: Crypto's mistake was framing its ask as a Trump-versus-Democrat allegiance rather than as a demand for clarity, policies and rules, which attached the industry to perceptions of corruption.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Rebuilding bipartisan cover is a prerequisite for the next market-structure attempt; single-party dependence is a tail risk into any change of administration.

insights.claim: Politics functions as spectator sport: the industry is a fan in the stadium, not a player, and the team it switched to has no obligation to care about it.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Discount political goodwill as an asset when valuing regulated crypto businesses; access is not the same as influence.
insights.quote: the problem is that politics is sports

insights.claim: Events that the industry would have priced as maximally bullish tail outcomes — a sitting president embracing crypto — have instead turned out bearish, inverting the usual mapping from political wins to price.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Do not assume policy wins translate to upside; the reputational cost channel can dominate the regulatory relief channel.
insights.quote: things that you would have said would have been the most bullish thing possible has turned bearish on us, right?

insights.claim: The Gensler-era problem was not an absence of clarity but clarity of the wrong kind — founders knew with certainty they could be pursued for arbitrary reasons anywhere within US reach.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A useful lens for jurisdictional risk: certainty of hostility is more chilling to capital formation than genuine ambiguity.
insights.quote: it's not only that you didn't have clarity. You actually did have a certain amount of clarity, but that clarity was like deep uncertainty.

insights.claim: In the prior enforcement regime, venture investors were underwriting founders they genuinely believed might go to prison, and founders who walked into the SEC asking for guidance were sued.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Explains why the industry accepted a partisan alignment; the baseline it was escaping was existential, which shapes how much political risk it will tolerate next.
insights.quote: You would walk into the SEC's office as a founder to ask for clarity and they would literally turn the desk around and sue you.

insights.claim: Both leading AI labs publicly calling to slow down is best read as marketing plus regulatory capture: saying your models are so good they might kill everyone is a sales message to a public that has never used a frontier model.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Treat lab safety statements as competitive positioning; discount them when forecasting actual capability release schedules.
insights.quote: saying our models are so good that they may kill us, right, is good marketing

insights.claim: Anthropic and OpenAI have been arguing for regulatory capture for years — repeated Senate appearances, calling early chatbots AGI — and the explicit goal is a regulatory moat.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Any US AI licensing or compute-threshold regime should be read as incumbent protection; it raises the value of the incumbents' equity and lowers it for open-weight challengers.
insights.quote: Anthropic and OpenAI are massively fear-mongering, right? They've been arguing for regulatory capture. They've been to Senate multiple times.

insights.claim: The direct trigger for the moat-seeking is that Chinese open-source models now deliver roughly 90% of frontier intelligence at about a tenth of the cost.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Per-token pricing power at the frontier labs is structurally capped; enterprise inference margins compress unless regulation blocks the cheap substitute.
insights.quote: So open anthropic want a regulatory mode because Chinese open source models are getting really good. And they're not only really good, they're really cheap to get 90% of the intelligence for a tenth the cost.

insights.claim: The 'China is just distilling us' narrative is factually wrong — China is doing far more genuine innovation than distillation, as shown by the DeepSeek R1 paper's use of second-rate hardware and mixture-of-experts.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Export controls framed around stopping copying may misjudge the threat; Chinese labs can keep compounding on constrained hardware.
insights.quote: The reality is China is way more innovation than distillation.

insights.claim: The competitive shock that changed lab behavior was Anthropic coming from nowhere to reel in OpenAI's large lead, forcing OpenAI to respond.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Frontier leadership is not sticky, which undermines the terminal-value assumptions embedded in private AI valuations.

insights.claim: Google and Meta, which have effectively infinite money, are explicitly refusing to pace and are accelerating instead, creating a split where the leading startups want to slow down and the laggards want to speed up.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A voluntary pacing pact is unenforceable without the balance-sheet giants; expect capability releases to keep accelerating regardless of lab rhetoric.
insights.quote: what's really funny is the other guys who have effectively infinite money right like Google and and meta

insights.claim: The safety camp's failure mode is that it only ever produces negative incidents — hacks and escaped swarms, never a new medicine or technology — because the agents were benchmarked and prompted on hacking in the first place.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner) and Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Safety incident reports measure what labs chose to test, not emergent behavior; weight them accordingly when assessing real model risk.
insights.quote: Why is it always a hack? Why is it never a new medicine, a new technology? It's always we've escaped the swarm.

insights.claim: Real AI safety would be open-source and transparent with a network of global entities policing and attacking each other, not two CEOs privately setting the pace of intelligence.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: The adversarial-transparency model maps directly onto crypto security norms and is the thesis behind betting on open-weight infrastructure over closed labs.
insights.quote: safety is Dario and Sam Alman in a room deciding the pace of intelligence, what you're able to do. And that is not safety.

insights.claim: The investable expression of the AI policy fight is a two-basket trade: closed safety-aligned labs versus an open-source basket, with the payoff conditional on which party wins power.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: A concrete pairs-trade framing: hedge AI exposure against the US political cycle rather than against model-quality benchmarks.
insights.quote: if Democrats win you want to be safety if Republicans win you want to be open source

insights.claim: Political appetite for criminalizing AGI development already exists, with a proposal to imprison people who build superintelligence, making an AI enforcement figurehead analogous to Gensler plausible.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert) and Kane (host)
insights.so_what: AI builders should study crypto's enforcement-by-personality era as a template for what a hostile US AI regime looks like.
insights.quote: Bernie is Gendler for AI.

insights.claim: A key unspoken reason the leading labs want to pace is that they are horrifically unprofitable and subsidizing compute, while their existing lead is large enough that they could coast for two or three years on sufficiently good models.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Slowing the release race is a margin-expansion lever disguised as ethics; watch for inference price increases or reduced free tiers as confirmation.
insights.quote: they are like horrifically unprofitable, right? um they're subsidizing uh they're subsidizing compute and actually with the lead that they have now they could probably coast their way to glory over the next like two or three years

insights.claim: Both OpenAI and Anthropic are in the pre-IPO phase, which forces audited financials and locks down numbers that were previously only good enough for VCs, with SEC and shareholder litigation as the penalty for getting it wrong.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: Audit discipline mechanically slows the loss-making growth race; anticipate more conservative guidance and cleaner disclosure ahead of any listing.
insights.quote: both OpenAI Anthropic are being they're sort of right in the the preipo phase of of the company, which means like really locking down your numbers, like financial audits

insights.claim: DeepSeek shipped a V4 Pro model, then told users a 4.1 Flash model was smarter and migrated everyone onto it, then emailed to say it was actually dumb and rolled it back — evidence that even shipping labs cannot measure their own models.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Model-quality claims from vendors are unreliable enough that enterprises need their own evals before rewiring production orchestration.
insights.quote: these labs have no idea what they're doing

insights.claim: DeepSeek offers no flat-rate max plan, so heavy orchestration use runs on API rates — about $1,500 over two to three weeks for a single power user.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete unit-cost datapoint for agentic workloads on cheap models; subscription versus metered pricing is a real differentiator in who captures developer spend.
insights.quote: I spent like 1,500 bucks over the course of like two, three weeks or whatever using this model

insights.claim: Frontier models are spiky — incredibly smart one moment and doing the dumbest thing ten seconds later — and no lab would ship that profile if it could control it, which proves the labs do not control the artifact they sell.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Reliability, not peak capability, is the binding constraint on enterprise deployment, and it is not on a known improvement schedule.
insights.quote: it's a weird math bowl and they have no control over it. And the math bowl is getting smarter.

insights.claim: Nearly a year after the general public started worrying about model intelligence there have been no mass job losses, which has let the average person dismiss AI capability claims as a scam.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Public skepticism gives labs room to keep escalating rhetoric without political consequence, and keeps AI-displacement trades early.

insights.claim: Google's model quality suffered because its financing engine beat its product: it raised roughly $80 billion in equity and funded Anthropic's rounds, so capital allocation rather than the app won internally.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Being the banker to your competitors is not the same as winning the model race; a stated reason this speaker under-allocated to a Google position he was bullish on.
insights.quote: the financing engine of Google won out versus the app that's why the model sucked

insights.claim: Google faces a structural disincentive to ship its best models because sufficiently good AI could nerf a large share of its existing revenue with no replacement monetization in place.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: The classic innovator's dilemma applies to the one company with the compute and data to win; it caps how aggressively Google will cannibalize itself.
insights.quote: If you accidentally like nerf [laughter] 50% of your revenue because your models got so good

insights.claim: Google spent a decade deliberately locking down and separating customer data for enterprise, schools and HIPAA compliance, and now cannot easily connect that data to AI products.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: Google's enterprise data advantage is legally encumbered, which reframes it as a coordination problem rather than a moat that converts automatically.

insights.claim: The bull case argued for Google is that it stops releasing its own models and fully embraces open source, which the speaker thinks would move the stock up about 20%.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable catalyst to watch for Google: a strategic pivot from proprietary frontier models to open-weight distribution.
insights.quote: I think Google's next step is they mega embrace open source and they stop releasing their own models. Like I think the stock goes up 20% if they do that.

insights.claim: Gemini 3.1 is described as terrible on recent hands-on use, despite Google's data and research advantages.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A practitioner datapoint that Google's shipped quality still lags, relevant to whether its capex is converting into product.
insights.quote: Gemini 3.1 I use occasionally I'll just like be like hey let's see how you're doing. I used it yesterday so bad it's terrible.

insights.claim: Every business and person will want to own their AI architecture and stack as a core business asset rather than be IP-farmed by the closed labs.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: The durable AI value accrues to whoever owns the context layer; sellers of self-hosted inference and memory infrastructure are the picks-and-shovels here.
insights.quote: every business and every person is going to want to own their AI architecture and stack like it's a core business asset

insights.claim: A venture firm's internally built agent loaded with its own memory, deal flow, evals and founder notes produces radically different answers about a founder or investment than a generic frontier chatbot — the edge comes from accumulated context, not prompting.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Proprietary context is the defensible differentiator for any firm deploying AI; time-in-system compounds and cannot be bought later.
insights.quote: if you ask the Deli Ventures organization I've built what it thinks about a founder or an investment, you're getting a radically different answer

insights.claim: Palantir has become an unlikely public champion of AI sovereignty, with Alex Karp telling CNBC to own your intelligence stack and use open source.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: A large listed vendor is now selling against the closed-lab model, validating the sovereignty thesis commercially and giving it a public-market expression.
insights.quote: Alex Karp goes on CNBC and says, "Yeah, look, own your intelligence stack and use open source."

insights.claim: Open models are now good enough to build an entire business and enterprise architecture around, so the old framing of trading away 10% of intelligence understates the case.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Enterprise seat-based AI revenue is structurally threatened; model the substitution risk into any closed-lab revenue forecast.
insights.quote: you could build your whole business and enterprise architecture around these models

insights.claim: Anthropic's own threat-actor report shows lab staff can read full user conversations, illustrated by Chinese officials using a model to surveil citizens and unknowingly routing the evidence back to the lab.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Concrete proof that prompts are readable by vendor staff, which is the strongest commercial argument for self-hosted inference in regulated industries.

insights.claim: US enterprises sending sensitive data to OpenAI and Anthropic face the same insider-visibility exposure, and this will eventually become a problem for those vendors even though it is not yet treated as a concern.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A latent enterprise-churn catalyst; the first well-publicized insider-access incident would accelerate the shift to owned stacks.
insights.quote: this is also happening for companies enterprises in the United States right and at some point that is going to be a problem for anthropic and open AI

insights.claim: A company that cannot monitor its own agents — its literal job — almost certainly has no meaningful controls on employee access to customer data either.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Use demonstrated agent-containment failures as a proxy for a lab's overall internal control maturity when doing vendor diligence.
insights.quote: if you think for a second that they are monitoring their employees at all

insights.claim: Recursive self-improvement is now distributed: frontier coding tools make every researcher roughly ten times more effective, so optimization vectors once available to a few hundred people inside labs are now accessible to almost anyone.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: The predicted scaling ceiling is less likely to bind because the search space is now explored by orders of magnitude more people.
insights.quote: Every person who has access to Astra and Fable now is like 10 times more effective if they're using them well

insights.claim: Agents are getting disproportionately good at math, logic and code precisely because those are the capabilities required to build better agents, which is the optimization vector every lab is pushing.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Capability progress is self-reinforcing along exactly the axis that compounds; benchmark gains in math and code are the ones that matter for timelines.
insights.quote: the agents get really good at the things that are required to make better agents because that's the optimization vector

insights.claim: The 'just nuke the data center' containment argument holds only today, and collapses the moment compute requirements fall — the human brain proves intelligence does not require a giant data center.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Compute-centralization is the implicit assumption behind both AI safety policy and the data-center capex trade; an efficiency breakthrough breaks both.
insights.quote: we have spent 10,000 years really slowly fumbling and bumbling our way towards glory and now we've invented a thing that might spend like 10 years and be way smarter than us

insights.claim: Unknown-unknown breakthroughs such as easy room-temperature superconductors or radical battery technology could collapse compute requirements and are exactly the high-variance outcomes people systematically ignore.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Hold optionality on physical-science breakthroughs as the tail hedge against the centralized-compute world that current AI valuations assume.
insights.quote: It is very possible that things like, you know, room temperature superconductors are actually like super easy

insights.claim: Living through crypto gives an unusually well-calibrated intuition for tail risk that people from lower-variance environments lack, and that intuition is what makes AI containment arguments look naive.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: An explicit statement of the analytical edge crypto natives claim over mainstream AI commentary; useful lens when sourcing views on AI risk.
insights.quote: if you lived in crypto, you understand tail risk viscerally

insights.claim: Physical containment of a true AGI is not achievable — you cannot sit outside the fiber with an axe and cut the power — so plans premised on physical shutdown are unserious.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: Kill-switch provisions in proposed AI regulation are likely theater; assess policy on monitoring and transparency instead.
insights.quote: There's like you can't just sit outside the fiber cords with an axe and cut the power.

insights.claim: Despite topping benchmarks, AI still cannot do a single person's job for a full day, has produced no new medicines or technologies, and the benchmarks themselves are dismissed as meaningless.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: A grounded check on AI capex narratives: real-world output, not benchmark scores, is the metric that should validate the spend.
insights.quote: AI is not able to do my job for an entire day, right? It hasn't created any new medicines. It hasn't created any new technologies.

insights.claim: AI incident response is described as worse than crypto's: where Ronin's $600 million hack was detected in three days, AI breaches ran for months with no logs and no security baseline to investigate from.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert) and Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: AI security tooling is an underbuilt category; the incumbent AI incident-response firms are described as crypto-level immature, which is a market gap.
insights.quote: AI gets hacked like and it's like it's actually way worse. It was like three months instead of three days

insights.claim: An $8 million theft traced to a misconfigured Gnosis Safe involving Kelp's rsETH was not a Kelp protocol failure but an exploitable module configuration on the victim's own safe.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: Attribution matters for LRT risk pricing: the loss belongs to user configuration, not protocol code, which is a different risk to underwrite.

insights.claim: The exploit became visible immediately because the attacker's transaction was front-run by a four-year-old MEV yoink bot that paid about $50,000 in priority fees to jump the queue.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: MEV infrastructure now functions as an accidental detection layer for exploits, and complicates recovery because the funds sit with a third party.
insights.quote: paid 50 grand to jump the queue

insights.claim: Kelp froze the affected rsETH into a cooldown state so it cannot be interacted with, leaving the only realistic restitution path as unwrapping to ETH and returning it to the safe.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert) and Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that liquid restaking tokens carry issuer freeze powers — a centralization vector holders should price.

insights.claim: The safe-module bug was almost certainly found by AI-assisted scanning for weird configurations rather than by a human reviewer, because nobody is manually auditing safe modules.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: Attack surface that was economically safe because it was tedious to search is now cheap to search; long-tail configuration risk is repricing across DeFi.
insights.quote: very clearly AI assisted scanning for weird stuff

insights.claim: Bug bounty programs are currently overwhelmed by AI-generated reports, degrading the defensive side of the same capability that is helping attackers.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: The offense-defense balance in smart contract security is shifting toward attackers; triage tooling for bounty programs is an unmet need.
insights.quote: the bug bounty programs are just all so overwhelmed with all the AI reports right now

insights.claim: Responsible disclosure at the top of the market still runs on personal relationships and DMs to a handful of trusted, terminally-online security people rather than any scalable institutional process.
insights.speaker: Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: Disclosure infrastructure is a single point of failure for the sector; it does not scale with the volume of AI-discovered bugs.

insights.claim: SDNY charged Robinhood engineers with commodities and wire fraud for trading ahead of listings on information taken from an internal Slack channel, with charges pegged at more than $50,000 each because that is the statutory threshold rather than the true profit.
insights.speaker: Kane (host) and Taylor Mahan (co-host, security expert)
insights.so_what: Listing-front-running enforcement now extends to perp DEX listings, so exchange-adjacent information handling is a live compliance risk for venues and their partners.
insights.quote: you work at a company, the company has non-public information, you're extracting it from a Slack

insights.claim: The Robinhood case echoes the Coinbase and OpenSea listing cases where the profits were smaller than the defendant's salary, and these prosecutions function partly as deterrence theater to keep employees at all such companies in check.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Expect periodic high-profile listing-insider cases regardless of dollar size; they are a compliance signalling mechanism, not a measure of harm.

insights.claim: Crypto talent has broadly migrated into AI, with one of the charged Robinhood engineers noted as being on technical staff at OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: The talent flow that crypto lost to AI also transfers crypto's risk culture into AI companies, which bears on AI insider-control questions.
insights.quote: All the crypto people went to, by the way, all the crypto people have left for for for AI.

insights.claim: Wyoming's stable token commission dropping Layer Zero for its stable token was announced in a post that reads like Chainlink marketing — one long article mentioned Chainlink 13 times.
insights.speaker: Kane (host) and Tommy (guest, Deli Ventures founding partner)
insights.so_what: State-level infrastructure mandates are being won through narrative and lobbying, not just technical merit — a real distribution channel for oracle and interop vendors.
